In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate. In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble.

Dentons is the largest law firm in the world by headcount, but it didn’t exist as such until 2013, when three separate firms, from three different countries, combined all at once to create it (its later mergers, including the 2015 Dacheng tie-up, only built on that foundation). items.title: Why Everything Looks Chaotic From The GC’s Desk
items.summary:
Imagine opening your inbox to a customer escalation, a product question, a contract exception, and a request for board materials. Each has a different owner. Each has a different deadline. All four need an answer today.

Now suppose they involve the same thing: the company has started describing an AI feature in a way its product documentation does not support.

Sales encounters the problem as a customer expectation. Product encounters it as an ambiguous requirement. Legal encounters it as contract language. The board encounters it as a question about oversight.

Four requests. One possible connection worth investigating.

That is the image behind a series I am calling “Above the Crossing.” Picture a GC standing amid the multidirectional movement of Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo. At street level, the most urgent task is avoiding the next collision. From a higher vantage point, routes and recurring points of convergence become easier to notice.

I use the image because a legal inbox organizes work by arrival. It offers very little help understanding how the work was produced.

A request that arrives on Thursday may have begun with a product decision made in February. Another request, arriving minutes later, may reflect a commercial commitment made yesterday. Their simultaneous arrival tells you almost nothing about their relationship.

Even the labels can get in the way. “Commercial,” “privacy,” and “product” are useful for assigning lawyers. They can separate matters that depend on the same fact, owner, or unresolved decision.

items.title: Realize Your Mistake Late — But Don’t Expect Us To Be Impressed
items.summary:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a hoot.

She was the wokest of the woke a half-dozen years ago, leading the charge for Woke 1: Defund the police. Don’t prosecute shoplifters. Avoid microaggressions. Defend the term “woke” itself against attacks.

But now she’s realized that Woke 1 went too far: “ Woke 1 was crazy. “

You don’t say.

Congratulations, AOC! You’ve caught on. But I’d rather support someone who was intelligent enough to see the truth all along.

I’m not ideological about this; it cuts in all directions.

Although Megyn Kelly was hardly the worst, she was only too willing to spread misleading electoral narratives in 2020 and 2021. But now, when Donald Trump tries to pull the same stunt and insist that the 2026 elections were stolen, she tells him to “ Just stop. “

Do tell.

Congratulations, Megyn!  You’ve caught on. But I’d rather hear opinion commentary from someone who was intelligent enough to see the truth all along.

Michael Cohen thought that Trump was the cat’s meow. And then he thought that Trump was a criminal who threatened democracy. And now he again thinks that Trump was OK. And in five years, when Trump’s inexplicable luster has vanished, Cohen will change his mind yet again.

Do people really listen to clowns like this?

I promise you that, within five or 10 years, you’ll be hearing from Republicans telling you that they’ve realized that Trump was a clownish buffoon all along.

Is that a fact?

Congratulations, Republicans! You’ll have seen the light.

But why didn’t you realize that Trump was a clownish buffoon from the very start? Wasn’t it obvious…
items.t: Realize Your Mistake Late — But Don’t Expect Us To Be Impressed

items.title: Biglaw Skipping 1L Interviews And Going Straight To Callbacks Before First-Semester Exams
items.summary:
Law firms started throwing the hiring cycle into disarray a few years ago, blowing off the tried and true on-campus interviewing regime to start recruiting in the middle of the academic year. As students and law schools complained about the incursion, the firms upped the ante, beginning to interview future lawyers before students even take first-semester exams. 

Now we’re hearing that at least a couple firms have gone further, eschewing initial interviews altogether and jumping straight to callbacks based on nothing but an application and vibes. Meanwhile, students have to show up to class in suits so they can bolt the moment the lecture ends. Which isn’t necessarily new, but we used to do that the first month of 2L fall. Meanwhile these students have to do it with their very first law school exams coming as early as three weeks from now .

According to one T14 tipster, the decision to jump right to callbacks beginning as early as this month caught students completely unaware. In fact, students started receiving links to sign up for callbacks within a week of sending in their applications. 

Which sort of does violence to the word “call back .”

Biglaw recruiting has morphed into the doomsday machine from Dr. Strangelove . Everyone agrees it’s insane . Bloomberg Law literally titled a podcast episode “ Everyone Hates Early Law School Recruiting, But Everyone Does It .” Morgan Lewis chair Jami McKeon told the outlet the firm is “absolutely” recruiting students before their first exams: “That’s what the market is right now, so you have to do it.”

There’s a lot about this…
items.t: Biglaw Skipping 1L Interviews And Going Straight To Callbacks Before First-Semester Exams

items.title: An Interview With David Pogue: AI Will Change A Lot. We’ll Cope.
items.summary:
I recently had the good fortune to interview David Pogue . Pogue is an Emmy-winning “CBS News Sunday Morning” correspondent, best-selling author, five-time TED speaker, and host of 20 “NOVA” science specials on PBS. He also served as The New York Times’ weekly technology columnist for 13 years. I wasn’t in Kansas anymore.

Pogue will speak on November 17 at Cleveland State University College of Law’s P. Kelly Tompkins Leadership and Law Center . His talk is entitled “AI: The Coping Crash Course” and is part of the Richard W. Pogue Leadership Conversation Series . And yes, there is a family connection. The lecture series is named for Richard W. Pogue, David’s father, a former managing partner of Jones Day . So, David isn’t exactly a stranger to legal.

He plans to discuss the current state of AI in general. And, according to the press release, what happens to evidence when realistic documents, photographs, and videos can be generated with a click.

We were joined in the interview session by Brian Ray . Ray is CSU Law’s co-interim dean, Baker Hostetler chair in law, and director of the Center for Cybersecurity and Privacy Protection . Ray knows a thing or two about AI himself.

Our discussion was informal, wide-ranging, and enlightening on a number of topics. It covered everything from deepfakes and AI slop to legal education, critical thinking, and the future of work. And the most important point was that AI is going to change a lot of things. But at the end of the day, we will cope.

items.title: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader Associates Are Getting Milbank Money
items.summary:
Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, the 3,100-lawyer firm created by the largest law firm merger in history , has told associates it will match the salary scale Milbank set back in June , plus the bonuses. The new scale runs from $235,000 for first-years up to $455,000 for the most senior associates, and it takes effect in January. Plus, the firm is matching Milbank’s bonuses too.

Then there’s the date. Milbank’s raises took effect July 1, so associates will finish 2026 on last year’s numbers. They have plenty of company: Goodwin , Winston Taylor , and a growing list of firms that match now and pay later . But it’s a change of pace for legacy Cadwalader. Back in 2021, Wall Street’s oldest firm matched Milbank’s raise the same afternoon Milbank announced it.

Still, a firm with more than $3.6 billion in revenue going full Milbank on both salary and bonuses matters. The summer standoff ended with mid-market firms dribbling in one at a time. Now one of the largest firms in the world is on board, and Cravath still hasn’t said a word. Year-end bonuses announcements are right around the corner, when we anticipate most firms will match. And if firms abstain from raises, well, not moving to the new salary scale is quickly becoming its own indicator.

items.title: Access To Justice Hackathon Kicks Off
items.summary:
Hackathons are generally built for speed. Folks gather for a weekend, an alarming quantity of pizza, and a slide deck promising to “disrupt” something. The compressed schedule is part of the process — taking people away from their daily concerns to focus on solving a problem through adrenaline and gumption.

The LawDroid Hackathon envisions more of a marathon than a sprint, which is more befitting the portmanteau. The virtual, global, open-source competition, announced in September, drew 50 submissions. Now, the five teams selected by a judging panel of LawDroid CEO Tom Martin, LawDroid Chief Legal Futurist Sateesh Nori, Lagniappe Law Lab Executive Director Amanda Brown, and LSNTAP Program Manager Shellie Reid will have until January to build tools to improve access to justice. 

In addition to the organizations represented on the panel of judges, the competition counts Legal Services Corporation , the Justice Technology Association , the ABA Center for Innovation , and Replit as partners.

“Each of these teams began with why,” Martin said, echoing this year’s theme of the legal tech awards he co-founded . “They know the people they serve and the problem they are solving, and they are building with purpose. I am especially proud of the broad coalition supporting this hackathon. When committed partners work together, good ideas have a real chance to make a positive difference in people’s lives.”

items.title: Did Cahill Gordon’s ‘Rescuer’ Get Revealed?
items.summary:
Last week , Biglaw’s favorite new parlor game was guessing who might swoop in for Cahill Gordon & Reindel. Monday brought two answers instead of one… and each came with its own website.

First, according to The Lawyer, a domain has been registered for a combined DLA Piper–Cahill firm as merger speculation around the 107-year-old Wall Street firm keeps mounting. Then Law.com reported that not only have domains pairing Cahill DLA been snatched up, but also domains linking Cahill with Willkie Farr & Gallagher have also been registered.

So, who’s the suitor?

A quick refresher: Cahill has lost eight finance partners this year, roughly 10% of its partnership. Last week, former ATL editor David Lat reported that the firm may be acquired . Lat didn’t name the buyer in his initial post, he described it only as much larger and more stable than Cahill, but with significantly lower profits per partner. (He did id DLA as the potential partner in his Judicial Notice post earlier this morning.)

If Willkie sounds familiar, it should. Willkie was on the other side of Weil’s merger talks, and those talks also became public after a pair of Weil-Willkie domain registrations turned up . Nothing says “we’re getting serious” like buying the joint URL. That deal died, and Weil is now winding down . Willkie, apparently, isn’t one to let a good domain-registration habit go to waste.

items.title: Listening to the past
items.summary:
Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded , but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

The role of history in text-and-history cases 

Originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

Sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary…
items.t: Listening to the past

items.title: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket
items.summary:
Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “ So Ordered .” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move quickly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he said, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”

Readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

The volume fell, but not to normal 

In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

For most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump…
items.t: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

items.title: How I survived being forced into pornography: ‘I died in that hotel room. I was a walking corpse’
items.summary:
In 2016, Mariah Rief, then 19, thought she was going to a modelling job at a hotel. Once there, she was sex trafficked. She knows of 15 fellow victims who have since died by suicide or drug overdose – and is determined to stop it ever happening again

When people ask Mariah Rief about her experience as a survivor of sex trafficking, they tend to start with the Craigslist ad which led the then 19-year-old to a “modelling shoot” at the Hilton hotel in San Diego. For others, the story starts when Rief enters the lobby and meets Theodore Gyi, the “photographer”. Or after they’ve taken the elevator up to a room, Rief standing at the threshold, Gyi behind her blocking her exit – and just inside the door, the silhouette of a second man waiting.

Whenever she talks about it, and whatever the questions, Rief always braces herself for blame, because, to some, it makes no sense. “You get, ‘But why did she answer that ad?’ ‘Why did she walk inside?’ and, my favourite, ‘Where were her parents?’” says Rief. “If you live in an idyllic world, it’s hard to imagine how this could happen.” The true starting point is years earlier. Rief’s beginnings, her childhood, layers of trauma and chaos, fast-tracked her to that hotel room in November 2016, believing that finally, life might be giving her a break. “It’s painful to say it but I was truly the perfect victim,” she says. “I saw that job as an opportunity. When I arrived at that hotel, I thought I was so lucky.”

Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks.

items.title: Stat(s) Of The Week: An Uneasy Relationship
items.summary:
As AI becomes increasingly integrated into legal practice, concerns about its impact remain. “Trust but verify” describes many attorneys’ approach to AI use, according to a new report that also highlights their concerns about job security.

Half of the lawyers surveyed for Bloomberg Law’s AI in Practice report said they trust AI tools enough to use them for complex tasks, and more than 40% said they turn to AI to test legal arguments before asking colleagues.

At the same time, 92% of attorneys said they verify each citation and quotation that AI produces. Many lawyers, including 36% of associates and 22% of partners, said they spend more time correcting AI analysis than doing analytical tasks.

And then there are the fears of AI agents going rogue or replacing humans. Three out of four attorneys said they are at least somewhat concerned about AI agents acting outside their expected parameters. And more than a third of associates (36%) and even 16% of partners fear they will lose their jobs to AI.

It’s happened over 2,000 times according to Damien Charlotin’s database . And when lawyers do it, they deserve to be called out. That’s old news. 

But what happens when lawyers use AI to write a brief that reads like AI slop? Or make arguments so nonsensical that you wonder whether they came from AI rather than a human being?

Well, that’s exactly what happened recently in a federal district court case in Texas, as reported in a Business Insider article . 

The Slop Order 

U.S. District Judge Mark Pittman ripped three lawyers to shreds not for hallucinated cases but for filing motions containing what he described as blatant AI slop, according to the article. 

The judge concluded the arguments were so weak and legally flawed that they must have been generated by artificial intelligence. He called the arguments relating to the meaning and interpretation of the statute tortured and tone-deaf. He labeled them superficially persuasive but said they subtly bent the law and had no merit. items.title: Many Lawyers Stopped Nickel-And-Diming Clients For Small Expenses
items.summary:
When I first started practicing law, attorneys at the law firm at which I worked needed to enter a billing code to complete many legal tasks. If an attorney wanted to make a telephone call, use the photocopier, or conduct legal research, the attorney needed to enter a client code so that the expense could be tracked and potentially passed along to the client. However, as technology has evolved and competition in the legal marketplace increased, many law firms have stopped charging clients separately for expenses that were once routinely included on legal bills.

One of the most obvious examples of this trend involves telephone charges. Decades ago, long-distance telephone calls could impose meaningful expenses on law firms, and it made some sense for firms to pass these costs along to clients. When I worked in Biglaw, attorneys needed to enter client codes when placing certain calls so that the firm could track the expense. However, most law firms now eat telephone charges rather than pass this cost onto clients, likely because law firms just pay flat rates for this service. Moreover, attorneys increasingly use cell phones and internet-based calling services to communicate with clients and other individuals involved in litigation. Under these circumstances, charging clients separately for routine telephone calls would seem strange, and many law firms no longer bother with such charges.

Photocopying expenses are another area in which law firms have changed their practices. Earlier in my career, attorneys and staff often needed to enter client codes when using photocopiers…
items.t: Many Lawyers Stopped Nickel-And-Diming Clients For Small Expenses

items.title: Judge Is Done Playing Nice With DOJ Over The Broadview Six
items.summary:
Judge April Perry has spent months trying to get a straight answer about what happened in the grand jury room in the Broadview Six case. The Department of Justice has spent those same months getting more and more creative about making sure she never gets one.

This week, Perry ran out of patience.

Quick refresher. Six protesters, including former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, were charged with felony conspiracy over a September 2025 protest outside the Broadview ICE facility in suburban Chicago. The case fell apart spectacularly in May , when prosecutors dropped all charges after Perry got a look at the grand jury transcripts. The transcripts showed that the first grand jury refused to indict, returning a “no bill.” So the prosecutor kept at it. She vouched for the case, talked substance with grand jurors outside the room, and excused the ones who disagreed with the government, until a later panel finally gave her the indictment. Perry said at the time, “I have never seen the types of prosecutorial behavior before a grand jury that I saw in those transcripts.” Then there’s the matter of what U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros knew and when, which didn’t exactly help his office’s credibility .

So Perry scheduled a hearing and asked Boutros and three line prosecutors to explain themselves. DOJ sent in Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward ( who has been making quite the name for himself this administration ) to make sure that never happens.

First, Woodward claimed that communications with the local prosecutors were privileged and off-limits to Perry’s inquiry.…

items.title: Tribal property and the Supreme Court
items.summary:
One of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights. From the first Supreme Court decisions in Indian affairs (such as Johnson v. McIntosh and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock ) , Indigenous property has been treated in a sui generis manner that is often to the detriment of Indigenous Peoples. Bryan Newland, assistant secretary for Indian Affairs in the Biden administration, recently delivered a major address in which he explained that the legacy of cases decided in the “ atmosphere ” of colonization remain impactful in 21st century litigation.

Before the court is a petition to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit’s decision in Chase v. Andeavor Logistics LP (now captioned Aubol v. Andeavor Logistics LP ), a trespass action by tribal citizen allotment owners against a pipeline company. Allotments are land parcels carved out of Indian reservations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The federal right-of-way allowing a pipeline in these Indigenous lands expired in 2013. The Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation has agreed to extend the right-of-way for its lands, but individual tribal citizens have not consented to the extension on their lands.

Though the pipeline company is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way. The cert petition argues that the 8th Circuit’s decision conflicts with the Supreme Court’s decision in…

items.title: What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race
items.summary:
Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff. 

***

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education . The case is one of several in recent years dealing with magnet school admissions policies. While prior cases addressed the constitutional permissibility of changes to selection criteria at some of the nation’s most sought after public high schools like the Thomas Jefferson High School in northern Virginia and Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science in New York City, this case addresses whether changes to selection criteria for middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.

In all of these cases, including this one, the policies at issue are facially neutral , meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard is not directly relevant. In that case, the court held that using race as an explicit factor in the admissions process was unconstitutional.

At issue in this case is a change from one facially neutral admissions policy to another. During the pandemic, the school adopted the so-called “Pandemic Plan.” Under the Pandemic Plan, all students are considered for admission to magnet schools if they meet minimum grade requirements and if their locally compared state assessment scores exceed…
items.t: What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

items.title: The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process
items.summary:
One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “ to be more fully informed .” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions? 

As noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not…

items.title: What Trump cases might soon return to the Supreme Court?
items.summary:
During the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats on two of his signature initiatives – his efforts to limit birthright citizenship and impose sweeping tariffs – as well as his initial attempt to fire Lisa Cook , a member of the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those issues. In the wake of the court’s decisions in each of the three cases, Trump continues to fight on, which has led (or could lead) to litigation that may reach the court again.

The Democratic Party’s decisive victory in the midterm elections, which gave it a majority in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, could theoretically hinder Trump’s plans. However, Democrats would need not just a majority to pass legislation curbing the president’s authority but a veto-proof majority: 67 votes in the Senate and 290 in the House, which could be more difficult to obtain.
items.t: What Trump cases might soon return to the Supreme Court?

items.title: Dangerous and unusual
items.summary:
Justice William O. Douglas announced his retirement on this day in 1975, more than 36 years into his tenure on the Supreme Court. Douglas is the longest-serving justice in Supreme Court history, though Justice Clarence Thomas will surpass Douglas’ record if he remains on the court through May 2028 .

At the Court The Supreme Court Building was closed on Wednesday for Veterans Day.

Tomorrow, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review . Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.
items.t: Dangerous and unusual
